    \end{equation}
    At the system default $\divpref = \tfrac{1}{2}$:
    \begin{equation}
        \boxed{
        \svdscore{p}\big|_{\divpref=1/2}
        = \prod_{e \in p}
          \underbrace{\detscore{e}}_{\text{coherence}}
          \cdot
          \underbrace{\sqrt{1+\tau_e^2}}_{\text{maturity}}
          \cdot
          \underbrace{\boltzfactor{\tentropy{e}}}_{\text{boundary}}
        }
        \label{eq:graph:half-score}
    \end{equation}
    Everything factorizes per edge: Dijkstra-compatible.  At this default the
    per-edge factor $\dampedweight{e}$ is the shared traversal primitive of
    \zcref{rem:epoch:shared-raw-edge-primitive}.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}[Default Rationale]
    \label{rem:graph:diversity-preference-default}
    The choice $\divpref = \tfrac{1}{2}$ is the unique value enabling
    Dijkstra factorization via $\sqrt{|\det|}$: the SVD score
    decomposes into a per-edge product (\zcref{eq:graph:half-score}),
    reducing matrix BFS ($\sim 25$ ops/edge) to scalar BFS
    ($\sim 8$ ops/edge).  It corresponds to the geometric mean of
    singular values, weighting dominant and recessive sentiment modes
    equally on the log scale.  It is also the unique value at which
    $\svdone{}^{1-\divpref}\svdtwo{}^\divpref$ is symmetric under
    $\svdone{} \leftrightarrow \svdtwo{}$, so the score does not
    privilege whichever singular value happens to be labeled dominant.
    This neutrality is appropriate for a system default.  The default
    is neutral between echo-chamber alignment ($\divpref \to 0$) and
    diversity preservation ($\divpref \to 1$).
\end{remark}

\paragraph{Limit cases.}
$\divpref = 0$: favors echo chambers (strongest mode).
$\divpref = \tfrac{1}{2}$: balanced (geometric mean, default).
$\divpref = 1$: favors diversity (weakest mode).

% ─── Extraction tiering ─────────────────────────────────────────────

\paragraph{Extraction tiering.}

At the system default $\divpref = \tfrac{1}{2}$, the SVD score
collapses to $\sqrt{|\det|}$, which factorises per edge.  The system
computes one $2 \times 2$ determinant and one sign test per edge ---
the entire per-edge computational footprint.  The full signed SVD is
the conceptual frame from which these two scalars descend; at the
default it is never instantiated per edge, and its richer quantities
are reconstructed only post-ranking for presentation.

\begin{table}[h!]
    \centering
    \caption{Extraction tiers of the signed SVD.  The per-edge tier
    is the entire computational footprint at $\divpref = \tfrac{1}{2}$.}
    \label{tbl:graph:extraction-tiering}
    \begin{tabular}{@{}l l l l@{}}
        \toprule
        \textbf{Tier} & \textbf{Quantities}
            & \textbf{When computed} & \textbf{Cost} \\
        \midrule
        Per-edge scalar (always)
            & $|\det|^{1/2}$, $\detsign{e}$
            & Every edge, both BFSs
            & ${\sim}\,1$ det $+$ 1 sign \\
        Post-ranking display
            & $\cohratio{p}$, $\modeangle{p}$
            & Displayed cards only
            & ${\sim}\,33$ ops/card \\
        Matrix BFS ($\divpref \neq \tfrac{1}{2}$)
            & $\svdone{}$, $\svdtwo{}$ individually
            & Never at the default
            & ${\sim}\,25$ ops/edge \\
        \bottomrule
    \end{tabular}
\end{table}

$\condnum{} = 1/\cohratio{}$ co-tiers with the coherence ratio
(zero marginal cost once $\cohratio{}$ is computed); the anisotropy
penalty (\zcref{def:graph:anisotropy-penalty}) uses it analytically,
not at runtime.

% ─── Path distance ───────────────────────────────────────────────────

\paragraph{Path distance.}

\begin{definition}[Path Distance]
    \label{def:graph:path-distance}
    At $\divpref = \tfrac{1}{2}$:
    \begin{equation}
        d(u, v)
        = \min_{p \in \mathrm{Paths}(u \to v)}
          \sum_{e \in p}
          \frac{1}{\detscore{e} \cdot \sqrt{1+\tau_e^2}}.
        \label{eq:graph:path-distance}
    \end{equation}
    Unlike the SVD path score (\zcref{def:graph:svd-path-score}), the
    boundary factor $\boltzfactor{\tentropy{e}}$ is \emph{intentionally
    absent}: the path distance uses raw internal edge costs
    (\zcref{ax:epoch:thermodynamic-boundary}).
\end{definition}

% ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
\subsection{Structural Properties}
\label{subsec:graph:structural-properties}
% ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

\begin{lemma}[Non-Vanishing Norm]
    \label{lem:graph:non-vanishing-norm}
    \necessityref{subsec:necessity:always-active-baseline}%
    $\norm{\symbf{\Psi}_e}_F \geq \fpl{1} \numrel{const.graph.fpl_baseline.num}$ for all
    edges (from the always-active baseline entry $\Psi^{22}$).
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Frobenius Bound]
    \label{lem:graph:frobenius-bound}
    $\norm{\symbf{\Psi}_e}_F \leq 3$.
    \proofsketch{9 entries, each bounded by 1.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proposition}[Polarization Floor]
    \label{prop:graph:polarization-floor}
    For any edge $e$ produced by the canonical pipeline:
    $\norm{\symbf{\Psi}_e}_F \geq \numval{const.graph.fpl_baseline.num}$ (\AttrView{}, from the
    always-active baseline, \zcref{lem:graph:non-vanishing-norm}) and
    $\Psi^{11} \geq \numval{const.graph.sigmoid_floor.num}$ (\PathView{}, since $a_{11} = 1$ for all
    domains and $\fpl{0} \numrel{const.graph.sigmoid_floor.num}$).
\end{proposition}

\begin{remark}[Path-Shortening Tendency]
    \label{rem:graph:path-shortening-tendency}
    For any 2-edge path $p$ terminating at content $c$ where
    $k_1 j_2 \geq 0$:
    $(P)_{11} \geq m_1 m_2 \geq 0.25$
    (\zcref{prop:graph:polarization-self-reinforcement}).  When the
    remaining entries are substantial, this raises $|\det P|$ and
    lowers the routing cost $1/\sqrt{|\det P|}$, shortening paths to
    high-polarization content.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Anisotropy Penalty]
    \label{def:graph:anisotropy-penalty}
    Per-edge log-cost difference between SVD and Frobenius scoring
    (diagnostic; only determinant scoring is operative in routing):
    \begin{equation}
        c_{\mathrm{SVD}}(e) - c_{\mathrm{Frob}}(e)
        = \tfrac{1}{2} \ln\!\bigl(
          \condnum{\pathview{e}}
          + 1/\condnum{\pathview{e}}
          \bigr).
        \label{eq:graph:anisotropy-penalty}
    \end{equation}
    This quantity does not enter any formula in \zcref{sec:sorting} or
    \zcref{sec:transport}; it characterizes how much additional
    routing cost the determinant-based scoring imposes on focused
    (high-$\kappa$) edges relative to a hypothetical Frobenius-based
    scoring that the system does not use. Numeric evaluations and proof are in
    \zcref{prop:sorting:anisotropy-penalty}.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[SVD Score Properties]
    \label{prop:graph:svd-score-properties}
    $\svdscore{p}$ is:
    (1)~strength-monotone ($\partial/\partial\svdone{} > 0$ for
    $\divpref < 1$);
    (2)~diversity-monotone ($\partial/\partial\svdtwo{} > 0$ for
    $\divpref > 0$);
    (3)~focus-penalizing ($\partial/\partial\condnum{} < 0$ for
    $\divpref > 0$);
    (4)~strictly positive whenever a viable path exists;
    (5)~weak-link suppressing: a single low-$\det$ edge
    $\epsilon \ll 1$ bounds the path score by
    $\sqrt{\epsilon} \cdot (\text{rest})$.
    \proofsketch{All from the product structure and SVD
    monotonicity.}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[Coherence Decay Bound]
    \label{prop:graph:coherence-decay-bound}
    The coherence ratio (\zcref{def:graph:coherence-ratio}) satisfies
    $\cohratio{p} \geq 1/\bar{\kappa}_G^{\,d}$, where
    $\bar{\kappa}_G = (\prod_e \condnum{e})^{1/d}$ is the geometric
    mean of edge condition numbers.  Path diversity decays at most
    exponentially.
    \proofsketch{From
    \zcref{cor:graph:condition-number-submultiplicativity}:
    $\condnum{P} \leq \prod_e \condnum{e}
    = \bar{\kappa}_G^{\,d}$.}
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Frobenius Upper Bound]
    \label{thm:graph:frobenius-upper-bound}
    $\svdone{\pathmatrix{p}}
    \leq \norm{\pathmatrix{p}}_F
    \leq \prod_e \norm{\pathview{e}}_F$.
    The gap measures energy lost to sentiment profile mismatches.
    \proofsketch{Spectral $\leq$ Frobenius; Frobenius is
    submultiplicative.}
\end{theorem}

% ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
\subsection{Path Diagnostics and Sentiment Archetypes}
\label{subsec:graph:path-diagnostics-and-archetypes}
% ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

The three diagnostic quantities $\detsign{p}$, $\cohratio{p}$,
$\modeangle{p}$ --- defined in
\zcref{subsec:graph:path-view-and-signed-svd} as extractions from any
$2 \times 2$ matrix and applied here to the composed path matrix
$\pathmatrix{p}$ (\zcref{def:graph:path-matrix}) --- jointly classify
paths into interpretable archetypes.  Classification is orthogonal to
the magnitude of the path score: two paths of the same archetype may
differ by orders of magnitude in $\sqrt{|\det(\pathmatrix{p})|}$.
The archetype describes \emph{how} sentiment transforms, not
\emph{how strongly}.

\begin{remark}[Path-Frame Convention]
    \label{rem:graph:path-frame-convention}
    For a composed matrix $\pathmatrix{p} = \pathview{e_1} \cdots
    \pathview{e_d}$, the left singular vectors defining $\modeangle{p}$
    live in the codomain of $\pathview{e_1}$ --- the first edge's
    intensity-mode coordinate system.  The archetype interpretations
    below are therefore anchored to the first edge's frame.  When the
    first edge is an Opinion (Tribal, full mask), the coordinate axes
    align with the net/signed and gross/unsigned intensity modes as
    defined in \zcref{def:graph:dominant-mode-angle}.  For paths whose
    first edge is a restricted-mask type (e.g.\ Affinity or Tag/A),
    the $\bleedparam$-softened entries dampen the off-diagonal
    coordinate axes, weakening the semantic interpretability of
    $\modeangle{p}$ without affecting its mathematical properties or
    its role in archetype classification.  The archetype names in
    \zcref{tbl:graph:sentiment-archetypes} are therefore most
    informative when the first edge carries a full bilinear mask.
\end{remark}

\begin{table}[h!]
    \centering
    \caption{Representative path sentiment archetypes (6 of 12
    possible $(\varrho, \epsilon, \vartheta)$ combinations).
    The six omitted cells --- including $(\text{high},\text{high})$,
    $(\text{low},\text{low})$, and $(\text{low},\text{mid})$ coherence--angle
    pairs at each parity --- are mathematically admissible but
    empirically rare for paths produced by the canonical pipeline.
    Each omitted cell is constructively reachable by choosing
    appropriate sequences of high- or low-$\condnum{}$ edges with
    controlled dominant-axis alignment; for instance,
    $(\text{low~}\cohratio{},\;\detsign{}=+1,\;
    \text{low~}\modeangle{})$ arises from consecutive
    high-$\condnum{}$ Tribal edges whose dominant axes are aligned
    with the signed intensity coordinate.
    All twelve combinations contribute identically to feed-ranking
    (given the same $\svdscore{}$) and to the raw signed double-cover
    service (subject only to whether $\detsign{p} = +1$).}
    \label{tbl:graph:sentiment-archetypes}
    \begin{tabular}{@{}l c c c p{4.8cm}@{}}
        \toprule
        \textbf{Archetype}
        & $\cohratio{}$ & $\detsign{}$ & $\modeangle{}$
        & \textbf{Interpretation} \\
        \midrule
        Aligned consensus
        & high & $+1$ & low
        & Community likes this and agrees about why. \\[4pt]
        Directed controversy
        & high & $-1$ & low
        & Strong engagement with inverted tribal signals.
          Cross-tribal bridge. \\[4pt]
        Enthusiastic agreement
        & low & $+1$ & high
        & Intense engagement in a coherent direction.
          Echo chamber of passion. \\[4pt]
        Intensity storm
        & low & $-1$ & high
        & Raw energy with inverted direction.
          Viral controversy without consensus. \\[4pt]
        Balanced exploration
        & high & $+1$ & mid
        & Both modes survive, faithful transmission.
          Healthy diverse engagement. \\[4pt]
        Confused inversion
        & high & $-1$ & mid
        & Both modes survive but direction inverts.
          Complex cross-tribal path. \\
        \bottomrule
    \end{tabular}
\end{table}

These quantities are computed post-ranking and do not enter any
scoring, standing, or CAN formula.  Their computational cost
(${\sim}\,33$ operations per displayed card) is discussed in
\zcref{rem:sorting:diagnostic-cost}.

% ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
\subsection{Aggregation and Hyper-Edges}
\label{subsec:graph:aggregation-and-hyper-edges}
% ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

\begin{definition}[Aggregated Sentiment]
    \label{def:graph:aggregated-sentiment}
    \necessityref{subsec:necessity:average-based-aggregation}%
    For $c \in V_c$ with in-neighborhood $N(c)$:
    $\bar{w}_c = |N(c)|^{-1}\sum_{u} w_{uc}$,
    $\bar{r}_c = |N(c)|^{-1}\sum_{u} r_{uc}$.
    Here $\bar{w}_c$ and $\bar{r}_c$ are local aggregated-sentiment averages.
    These feed into \zcref{def:graph:sentiment-slice} to produce a
    node-level $3 \times 3$ matrix.  The scalar content norm
    $\norm{\symbf{\symcal{T}}_c}_F$ enters the relevance score
    (\zcref{def:sorting:relevance-score}).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Hyper-Edge Scalar Interface]
    \label{def:graph:hyper-edge-scalar-interface}
    For a complete hyper-edge act $\symcal{H}$ with matched legs
    $e_{ap}$ and $e_{ph}$:
    \[
        \norm{\symbf{\symcal{T}}_{\symcal{H}}}_F
        \coloneqq
        \norm{\symbf{\symcal{T}}_{e_{ap}}}_F
        \cdot
        \norm{\symbf{\symcal{T}}_{e_{ph}}}_F.
    \]
    This is a \emph{consistency identity} for raw-leg consumers: when a
    feed, raw bridge, or path-diagnostic computation expands the
    hyper-edge into its A-leg and T-leg (each counted individually
    toward the raw path length bound $L$), the product of leg norms
    equals the expanded traversal contribution.  The aggregate scalar is
    not itself consumed by any formula in \zcref{sec:sorting,sec:transport}
    (\zcref{tbl:graph:consumer-map}).

    It is not a standing coefficient.  Standing consumes a
    standing-designated hyper-edge only as the complete act of
    \zcref{def:graph:act-edge-projection}; no leg is independently traversable,
    and the relation coefficient is defined with the standing
    projection in \zcref{sec:epoch}.  For hyper-leaf nodes used as
    content termini, the aggregated content scalar
    $\norm{\symbf{\symcal{T}}_c}_F$
    (\zcref{def:graph:aggregated-sentiment}) remains the relevant
    quantity, computed from the node's incoming edges, not from this
    product.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Hyper-Edge Reduction]
    \label{thm:graph:hyper-edge-reduction}
    Any complete hyper-edge act
    $\symcal{H}=(e_A,e_T)$ satisfies four consumer-specific reductions:
    \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
        \item \textbf{Raw scalar.}
              $\norm{\symbf{\symcal{T}}_{\symcal{H}}}_F
              =
              \norm{\symbf{\symcal{T}}_{e_A}}_F
              \norm{\symbf{\symcal{T}}_{e_T}}_F$
              (\zcref{def:graph:hyper-edge-scalar-interface}).

        \item \textbf{Raw \PathView{}.}
              The expanded raw path matrix is
              $\pathview{\symcal{H}}
              =
              \pathview{e_A}\pathview{e_T}$, hence
              \[
                  \det(\pathview{\symcal{H}})
                  =
                  \det(\pathview{e_A})
                  \det(\pathview{e_T}),
              \]
              and
              $\detsign{\symcal{H}}
              =
              \detsign{e_A}\detsign{e_T}$
              by \zcref{cor:graph:path-parity-sign}.

        \item \textbf{\AttrView{}.}
              Each leg supplies an independent CAN base value.  The
              complete hyper-edge induces the depth-1 composition node
              of \zcref{def:can:dependency-induction}, with
              $\redundancy{}=1$.

        \item \textbf{Standing consumer.}
              If and only if the closed person-vouch census designates
              the family and the act is complete, standing consumes
              $\symcal{H}$ once as one actor-authored semantic act.
              Neither leg is a standing edge, no raw path may enter the
              T-leg independently, and no unrelated incoming edge may
              substitute for the matched A-leg.  The middle passive
              artifact remains contextual and is absent from the
              projected standing path.
    \end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
    Clauses~1 and~2 are the scalar identity and determinant
    multiplicativity of the expanded raw legs
    (\zcref{def:graph:hyper-edge-scalar-interface,%
    thm:graph:determinant-product}).  Clause~3 is Rule~2 of
    \zcref{def:can:dependency-induction}.  Clause~4 follows from the
    complete-act identity and co-leg checks of
    \zcref{def:graph:act-edge-projection}: a standing consumer is defined on the
    act identity, not on either leg's independently reachable graph
    position.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Standing Act Atomicity]
    \label{cor:graph:standing-act-atomicity}
    For any standing-designated hyper-edge family, the standing
    projection receives the complete matched act or receives nothing.
    An unmatched T-leg, an unmatched A-leg, an unrelated incoming edge
    to the middle artifact, an independently folded leg bundle, or a raw
    path prefix contributes zero standing through that act.

    This is an interpretation property and is distinct from admission
    leg atomicity
    (\zcref{cor:graph:act-projection-atomicity}), which states only that
    the two records are written together.
\end{corollary}

% ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
\subsection{Interaction Domains and Mask Rationalization}
\label{subsec:graph:interaction-domains}
% ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Edge parameters cluster into conceptual domains.  The domain determines
the default binary mask; the mask rationalization promotes edges whose
parameters are signed directional quantities.

\begin{table}[h!]
    \centering
    \caption{Interaction domains. Parameters shown are representative; the Edge
    Census (\zcref{tbl:nodes:archetype-fingerprints}) is normative per edge.}
    \label{tbl:graph:interaction-domains}
    \begin{tabular}{@{}l l c l@{}}
        \toprule
        \textbf{Domain} & \textbf{Parameters}
            & \textbf{Default mask} & \textbf{Tier} \\
        \midrule
        Tribal
            & polarity, reaction, enthusiasm
            & $(1,1,1,1)$ & \tierfull{} \\
        Epistemic
            & confidence, effort, relevancy
            & $(0,1,0,1)$ & \tiermarginal{} \\
        Economic
            & generosity, urgency, attachment
            & $(0,0,1,1)$ & \tiermarginal{} \\
        Relational
            & formality, responsibility, equity
            & $(0,0,1,1)$ & \tiermarginal{} \\
        Identity
            & (standing-derived)
            & $(1,0,0,1)$ & \tierfull{} \\
        Minimal
            & (bare activity)
            & $(0,0,0,1)$ & \tiermarginal{} \\
        \bottomrule
    \end{tabular}
\end{table}

\emph{Note.}  The column lists the default routing tier of an
unpromoted edge.  Mask promotion lifts Owner, Participant, and Send/A to
\tierfull{}; the settlement and proposal edges route at \tierhalf{}
(\zcref{def:graph:mask-promotion-criterion,%
def:graph:proposal-half-tier}).

\begin{definition}[Mask Promotion Criterion]
    \label{def:graph:mask-promotion-criterion}
    An edge whose parameters are signed ($p \in [-1,1]$) and whose
    sign expresses a \emph{stance toward the target} --- agreement vs.\
    opposition, enthusiasm vs.\ reluctance, comfort vs.\ discomfort ---
    has its mask promoted to $(1,1,1,1)$, regardless of conceptual
    domain. A signed parameter whose sign is a \emph{self-report about
    the author's own relation to the target} does not promote: Affinity
    (association, attraction) is the standing counterexample ---
    relevance, not verdict. Where the reading is contestable, the Edge
    Census (\zcref{rem:nodes:edge-census-normative}) governs.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Proposal Half-Tier Assignment]
    \label{def:graph:proposal-half-tier}
    \necessityref{subsec:necessity:settlement-half-routing}%
    \necessityref{subsec:necessity:proposal-half-tier}%
    A signed-stance edge whose primary effect awaits a counterparty's own
    authored act routes at the \tierhalf{} tier. Two families are exactly
    these: the settlement handshake (Bid, Accept, Ratify --- title
    recognition and transfer are sentiment-blind,
    \zcref{thm:graph:epoch-title-fold,rem:graph:settlement-reputation}, so
    their signed parameters tint commercial reputation but must not carry
    primary routing force) and the conversational proposals (Join Request,
    Invitation --- membership exists only through a Participant edge
    authored by the joining actor,
    \zcref{rem:nodes:chat-proposals-do-not-participate}). Proposals carry a
    genuine directional stance and retain a full stored block; the
    \tierhalf{} floor applies in the path view only and, by
    \zcref{lem:graph:tier-floor-sign-invariance}, preserves every proposal
    determinant sign.
\end{definition}

Three edges are promoted to a full stored block and route at
\tierfull{}: Owner, Participant, and Send/A.  The settlement edges
Bid/A, Bid/T, Accept, and Ratify and the proposal edges Join
Request and Invitation/A carry a full stored block but route at
\tierhalf{} (\zcref{def:graph:proposal-half-tier}).
The criterion: the parameter's sign
carries
meaningful directional information (agreement vs.\ opposition,
enthusiasm vs.\ reluctance, comfort vs.\ discomfort).
See \zcref{tbl:nodes:archetype-fingerprints} for the complete listing.

Bid edges carry a full stored block and route at \tierhalf{}
($g \in [-1,1]$ signed generosity,
$u \in [0,1]$ urgency).  The sign of generosity carries
directional information --- generous ($g > 0$) versus predatory
($g < 0$) --- so the Bid satisfies the mask promotion criterion
(\zcref{def:graph:mask-promotion-criterion}) on genuine directional
grounds: the signed parameter encodes a stance rather than inflating a
single non-negative scalar functional.  The signed Bid
carries a meaningful determinant sign $\detsign{e_{\mathrm{Bid}}}$
consumed by the settlement reputation rule
(\zcref{rem:graph:settlement-reputation}).
The \tierhalf{} floor leaves $\detsign{e_{\mathrm{Bid}}}$ exactly as in
\zcref{lem:graph:tier-floor-sign-invariance}, so the settlement
reputation rule (\zcref{rem:graph:settlement-reputation}) is unaffected.

\zcref{sec:nodes} specifies every node and edge type that
instantiates this machinery, together with each type's participation in
both views.

% ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
\subsection{Settlement Lifecycle and Ownership Thread}
\label{subsec:graph:settlement-lifecycle}
% ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Ownership of an Item is not a stored attribute.  It is a derived quantity:
the buyer of the first completed purchase in a causal chain of recognized
settlements, each settlement itself a pattern matched over independently
authored edge records.  Five edge families --- three forward (Bid, Accept,
Ratify) and two cancel (Withdraw, Rescind) --- span the complete lifecycle
of an Item transfer.  Every state transition is caused by an authored
edge; no state changes through inaction, counting, or timeout
(\zcref{thm:graph:no-death-by-inaction}).  The lifecycle follows the
three-way handshake: buyer proposes (Bid), seller responds with consent
and counterterms (Accept), buyer confirms and commits (Ratify); each party
holds a cancel record in every non-terminal state where it has standing.
Commitment is \emph{epoch-quantized}: the buyer's Ratify proposes the
commit, and the commit \textbf{finalizes at the first epoch boundary} at
which it stands unchallenged (\zcref{post:graph:title-act-bundle-reservation}).
Within an epoch there is no ``who was first'': title reads epoch membership,
never sub-epoch order.

\begin{definition}[Item Genesis Act]
    \label{def:graph:item-genesis-act}
    An Item~$n_i$ enters the graph together with an initial Owner edge
    $\mathrm{Actor}_{a_0} \to n_i$ authored by its originating
    actor~$a_0$.  This Owner edge is the \emph{genesis} of the ownership
    thread of~$n_i$ (\zcref{def:graph:ownership-thread}): it is the thread
    root, has no preceding settlement, and establishes $a_0$ as the first
    certified owner.  The genesis edge is an ordinary user-authored
    $V_u$-sourced edge (\zcref{ax:graph:passivity}, clause~(a)).
    \textbf{Item identity is declarative} (the Minted-class rule of
    \zcref{def:graph:node-taxonomy}, of which the Item is the original
    instance): the Item \emph{is} its genesis act --- its identity is minted
    from the genesis act identifier $\actid{q}$
    (\zcref{def:graph:act-identifier}), the same act identity that settlement
    references resolve to (\zcref{def:graph:settlement-act-reference}).
    Uniqueness holds by construction: a
    colliding act identifier is author-equivocation, rejected by record integrity
    (\zcref{post:introduction:record-integrity}), never adjudicated by
    title logic; two actors listing ``the same'' referent create two
    Items with two ownership threads, so contested genesis is
    structurally impossible and the conservative void at the root
    (\zcref{def:graph:title-certificate}) handles only record-integrity
    edge cases. No payload datum enters the act identifier
    (\zcref{def:graph:act-payload-projection}), so identity, resolution, and
    title survive every payload state. The residual question --- whether
    a registered Item corresponds to a real-world referent, and which of
    two listings does --- is out-of-band by the gauge argument
    (\zcref{ins:introduction:the-cut-no-mechanism-can-make}), deterred by
    accountability cost, and witnessed at
    \zcref{frontier:item-genesis}. The
    genesis edge is an ordinary gated append: $a_0$ must satisfy the write rule
    of \zcref{post:epoch:final-act-sequence-write-rule}.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}[A Named Limit on Title]
    \label{rem:graph:item-identity-limit}
    In the register of \zcref{ins:introduction:the-floor-we-name}: title
    at Layer~1 is title over a \emph{registered claim}, never custody of
    a referent. Ownable means the claim is transferable under
    recognition; whether the sneaker exists, and which listing is the
    real one, is the community's to check --- the same out-of-band look
    that makes the cut no mechanism can make. This mirrors the payload
    limit: the edge's authorship is always provable, the payload's only
    above Layer~1; the claim's title is always derivable, the referent's
    only outside it.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Settlement Act Reference]
    \label{def:graph:settlement-act-reference}
    The Accept and Ratify acts --- and only these --- each carry an act-level
    public protocol reference to the \textbf{Bid act
    identifier}~$\actid{q_{\mathrm{Bid}}}$ that opened the Offer under
    negotiation:
    \[
        \operatorname{settles}(q_{\mathrm{Accept}})=\actid{q_{\mathrm{Bid}}},
        \qquad
        \operatorname{settles}(q_{\mathrm{Ratify}})=\actid{q_{\mathrm{Bid}}},
    \]
    and a Ratify additionally references the exact Accept act identifier it
    confirms,
    $\operatorname{accepts}(q_{\mathrm{Ratify}})=\actid{q_{\mathrm{Accept}}}$.
    These references are act-owned \emph{metadata, not graph incidence}: an
    Accept or Ratify names its settlement partner by act identity, not by the
    Bid/T edge-projection key, and its edge projection is incident only to its
    two actor endpoints, never to the Offer it references.  This keeps the
    Offer's incident set minimal: commits and cancels are mutually independent
    acts, consumed only by the recognition predicate
    (\zcref{rem:graph:title-order-irrelevance}).  The references imply
    $q_{\mathrm{Bid}}\causalparent q_{\mathrm{Accept}}\causalparent
    q_{\mathrm{Ratify}}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Authored-Act Causal Parents]
    \label{def:graph:act-causal-parents}
    An authored act may declare \emph{asserted parents}: a set of prior-act
    references, as a structural field of its body $\actbody{q}$.  They define
    the \emph{causal-parent relation}
    \[
        p \causalparent q
        \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
        q \text{ asserts } p \text{ as a prior act},
    \]
    which is directed and acyclic: backward-only by construction (a reference
    cites a formed act), and acyclic within a submission batch by the
    topological formation check of \zcref{def:network:admission-closure}.
    Semantics: the act is admissible only into an epoch that contains, or whose
    history contains, every asserted parent earlier --- this act must be after
    those acts. The \texttt{settles}-pointer
    (\zcref{def:graph:settlement-act-reference}) is the settlement family's instance of
    this field, with its family-specific resolution semantics unchanged. Like
    the \texttt{settles}-pointer, an asserted parent is metadata, not graph
    incidence. The causal-parent relation \emph{orders} acts; it is distinct
    from the shared parent act of a hyper-edge's two projections
    (\zcref{def:graph:dependent-act-set}), which \emph{groups} them without
    ordering them.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Dependent Authored-Act Set]
    \label{def:graph:dependent-act-set}
    An authored act's admission is constrained by the directed acyclic
    \emph{causal-parent} relation $\causalparent$
    (\zcref{def:graph:act-causal-parents}), and its two edge projections are
    admitted together because they share one parent act,
    \[
        \actof{e_A}=\actof{e_T}=q .
    \]
    This shared-parent grouping is not a directed parent: it imposes no order
    between the projections --- they carry one act identifier and, once
    accepted, one authoritative time --- and it is exactly the formation of
    \zcref{def:graph:act-edge-projection}.  A retrieved projection that names a
    missing, wrong-family, wrong-author, or wrong-role sibling belongs to no
    formation-valid act.  Causal parents order acts; the shared parent binds a
    hyper-edge's projections; neither is a reservation over records its author
    did not write, so both are backward-only in effect and no forward
    constraint exists.

    A \emph{dependent set} is a set $S$ of formed acts closed under the
    causal-parent relation --- every causal ancestor ($\causalparent$) of every
    member is either already written or itself in $S$ --- taken together with
    both edge projections of every hyper-edge act in $S$.  Grouping a
    hyper-edge's projections by their shared parent act, rather than by a
    mutual parent, keeps the causal-parent graph acyclic while still admitting
    both projections together.  Minimal dependent sets are the closures of a
    single act; any larger candidate decomposes into them. The dependent set
    is the sole unit of the write: written whole or not at all
    (\zcref{def:network:write}). No further closure is needed --- in
    particular, no same-author generator: an unwritten act has no existence,
    so the order of any written subset is complete over that subset, and the
    identity chain of \zcref{lem:graph:act-edge-identifier-uniqueness} runs over written acts
    only. This is the closure that
    \zcref{subsec:necessity:conflict-not-causal} already isolated: causal
    parents and the shared parent act, nothing else.
\end{definition}

\begin{corollary}[Authored-Act Projection Atomicity]
    \label{cor:graph:act-projection-atomicity}
    A hyper-edge's A-projection and T-projection share one parent act,
    $\actof{e_A}=\actof{e_T}=q$ (\zcref{def:graph:dependent-act-set}), so they are
    the single unit of one act's write; they are written whole or not at all.
    Because they are grouped by their shared parent rather than by a mutual
    parent, admitting both projections together creates no causal cycle.

    This is an admission property only.  It does not authorize a
    downstream consumer to traverse or interpret either leg
    independently; the standing-consumer consequence is
    \zcref{cor:graph:standing-act-atomicity}.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}[Dependency Closure Excludes Conflicts]
    \label{rem:graph:dependency-closure-excludes-conflicts}
    Conflict grouping by causality is rejected. Cancels and commits are
    concurrent by construction: the settlement-reference independence of
    \zcref{def:graph:settlement-act-reference} creates the regret window, and no
    dependency closure can co-transport them. Conflict protection is the
    boundary-accountability rule (\zcref{post:graph:boundary-accountability}),
    not write-unit grouping. Widening the dependent set to include conflicts would
    require either mandatory cross-references, destroying the regret window, or
    a serialization choice function, corrupting title; the dependent set is
    already its closure.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Public Protocol Reference]
    \label{def:graph:public-protocol-reference}
    A \emph{public protocol reference} is a non-removable structural field
    required to identify the meaning or validity of an authored act: the
    hyper-edge A/T role and shared act identifier
    (\zcref{def:graph:act-identifier}); the \texttt{settles}-pointer
    (\zcref{def:graph:settlement-act-reference}); Ratify's reference to the exact Accept
    it confirms; structural target and incidence fields; family-required
    prior-act references; license qualifiers; and other public formation
    metadata.  Public protocol references remain in the structural record after
    every payload or dependency tombstone and are always available for
    formation replay, title recognition, complete-act reconstruction, and public
    semantic interpretation.  They are distinct from the removable
    Actor-authored dependency list (\zcref{def:graph:act-dependency-projection}):
    public protocol references identify \emph{what} an act is; Actor-authored
    dependencies constrain \emph{where} the host may place it.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Act Removable Projections]
    \label{def:graph:act-removable-projections}
    Every authored act (\zcref{def:graph:authored-act}) may carry two typed
    removable projections --- a \emph{content} projection and a
    \emph{dependency} projection --- each governed by the separable, concealing
    commitment of \zcref{post:graph:separable-act-projections}: full bytes and
    opening material beside carriage, a binding-yet-concealing commitment
    residue in the structural record, and one-way tombstoning that leaves the
    structural act immutable.  Their semantics differ only in read-site: the
    content projection is never read at Layer~1, whereas the dependency
    projection is read by the host at admission to validate order
    (\zcref{def:graph:authoritative-act-order}).  The commitment residue of each is a
    normative structural field retained across tombstoning.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Act Dependency Projection]
    \label{def:graph:act-dependency-projection}
    For an authored act $q$, the Actor chooses a finite canonical dependency set
    \[
        \actdeps{q}=\set{\actid{p_1},\ldots,\actid{p_m}},
    \]
    each element naming one authored act (\zcref{def:graph:act-identifier}),
    never one individual leg, and declaring that $q$'s authoritative time must
    exceed each $p_j$'s.  The encoding is sorted by act identifier, duplicate-free,
    self-dependency-free, bounded in count and byte length, and versioned; the
    canonical empty list is valid and distinct from a missing one.  The
    declaration grants no inclusion right: if a dependency is unavailable or the
    declared order is unsatisfiable, the host may omit $q$
    (\zcref{def:network:write}).  The projection carries the list and its opening
    material in one of three states, moving one-way toward tombstoned:
    \begin{description}[nosep]
        \item[\textnormal{full-empty}] $\actdeps{q}=\varnothing$ with opening present;
        \item[\textnormal{full}] the canonical list and opening present;
        \item[\textnormal{tombstoned}] list and opening removed from Layer-1
            carriage, the binding dependency commitment residue remaining.
    \end{description}
    The retained commitment binds one canonical list to the act, and is the
    anchor a later opening reopens.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Act Dependency Tombstone]
    \label{def:graph:act-dependency-tombstone}
    Tombstoning the dependency projection removes only the dependency list, its
    opening material, and Layer-1 carriage responsibility for those values.  It
    changes none of: authored-act identity, edge-projection identity, authoritative
    order and logical time, action count, debit, accepted edge set, act
    edge-projection formation, standing, feed, bridge transport, CAN, title, settlement
    recognition, or the retained dependency commitment.  A dependency tombstone
    is therefore not record deletion; like the payload transition
    (\zcref{def:graph:act-payload-state}) it is a one-way carriage change over an
    immutable structural act.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Proposal Pre-Commitment]
    \label{def:graph:proposal-pre-commitment}
    Because the host contributes the final projection salts, the Actor first
    binds its proposal.  Let $\actbody{q}$ be the canonical Actor-chosen structural body
    of proposed act $q$ --- act identifier, author, family, binary/hyper-edge
    shape, incidence, authored semantic coordinates, public protocol references
    (\zcref{def:graph:public-protocol-reference}), and the requested content-
    and dependency-projection publication states --- excluding all host salts,
    residues, seals, epoch index, and logical time.  With content bytes $\actpayload{q}$,
    canonical dependency encoding $\operatorname{encode}(\actdeps{q})$, and a fresh
    private proposal nonce $\propnonce{q}$, define the projection pre-digests
    \[
        h^{\mathrm{pre}}_{\mathrm{content}}(q)
        =H\!\left(\textsf{PN-content-pre-v1}\parallel\actid{q}
        \parallel \propnonce{q}\parallel \actpayload{q}\right),
        \quad
        h^{\mathrm{pre}}_{\mathrm{dep}}(q)
        =H\!\left(\textsf{PN-dependency-pre-v1}\parallel\actid{q}
        \parallel \propnonce{q}\parallel\operatorname{encode}(\actdeps{q})\right),
    \]
    and the Actor-signed \emph{proposal pre-commitment}
    \[
        \precommit{q}
        =H\!\left(\textsf{PN-act-proposal-v1}\parallel\operatorname{encode}(\actbody{q})
        \parallel h^{\mathrm{pre}}_{\mathrm{content}}(q)
        \parallel h^{\mathrm{pre}}_{\mathrm{dep}}(q)\right),
        \qquad
        \presig{q}=\operatorname{Sign}_{\operatorname{author}(q)}
        \!\left(\precommit{q}\right).
    \]
    It exists before host salting, binds the exact proposal, content, dependency
    list, and requested publication states, cannot be transplanted to another
    act identifier, carries no host order, and grants no inclusion.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Verified Act]
    \label{def:graph:verified-act}
    On a proposal $\bigl(\actbody{q},\actpayload{q},\actdeps{q},\propnonce{q},\precommit{q},
    \presig{q}\bigr)$ the host verifies the Actor signature,
    act-identifier uniqueness, canonical formation, hyper-edge A/T consistency,
    public protocol references, carriage and dependency bounds, absence of
    self-dependency, and the recomputed pre-commitment.  A failure produces no
    Layer-1 object.  The host then chooses independent fresh salts
    $\payloadsalt{q},\actdepsalt{q}$ (distinct, domain-separated,
    meeting the published entropy floor) and forms the binding commitments
    \[
        \payloadcommit{q}=H\!\left(\textsf{PN-content-v1}\parallel
        \actid{q}\parallel \precommit{q}\parallel
        \payloadsalt{q}\parallel \actpayload{q}\right),
    \]
    \[
        \actdepscommit{q}=H\!\left(\textsf{PN-dependency-v1}\parallel
        \actid{q}\parallel \precommit{q}\parallel
        \actdepsalt{q}\parallel\operatorname{encode}(\actdeps{q})\right).
    \]
    The \emph{verified act} is the header
    \[
        \verifiedact{q}=\bigl(\actbody{q},\precommit{q},\presig{q},
        \payloadcommit{q},\actdepscommit{q},v_{\mathrm{content}},
        v_{\mathrm{dep}}\bigr),
    \]
    with edition tags $v_{\mathrm{content}},v_{\mathrm{dep}}$ and no host order
    fields, sealed by
    $\verifyseal{q}=\operatorname{Sign}_{\mathrm{host}}
    (H(\textsf{PN-verified-act-v1}\parallel\operatorname{encode}(\verifiedact{q})))$.
    The seal attests receipt, pre-commitment verification, formation validity,
    and salt addition; it promises no inclusion.  The host returns
    $\bigl(\verifiedact{q},\payloadsalt{q},\actdepsalt{q},
    \verifyseal{q}\bigr)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Approval Witness and Eligibility]
    \label{def:graph:approval-witness}
    Before approving, the Actor verifies the host seal; exact equality of the
    returned $\actbody{q}$, act identifier, semantic coordinates, public protocol
    references, requested projection states, $\precommit{q}$, and
    $\presig{q}$; correct opening of $\payloadcommit{q}$ to
    $\actpayload{q}$ and of $\actdepscommit{q}$ to $\actdeps{q}$; correct editions; and, for a
    hyper-edge, agreement of all act-level fields across both legs.  On success
    the Actor signs the \emph{approval witness}
    \[
        \approvewitness{q}=\operatorname{Sign}_{\operatorname{author}(q)}
        \!\left(H\!\left(\textsf{PN-act-approval-v1}\parallel\operatorname{encode}(\verifiedact{q})
        \parallel\verifyseal{q}\right)\right),
    \]
    approving this exact verified act, including its host-added content and
    dependency commitments, as the accepted realization of the precommitted
    proposal.  The witness signs no epoch index, position, logical time,
    final-set membership, standing, or title outcome.  Only a verified act with
    a valid approval witness is eligible for host ordering; the host must reject
    from candidate ordering any act with an absent or invalid witness, a header
    differing from the signed one, a hyper-edge leg differing at an act-level
    field, a dependency opening that no longer matches, or a dependency set
    unsatisfiable in the proposed sequence.  A verified but unaccepted act
    remains off-record submission state.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Ordering Fraud Proof]
    \label{def:graph:ordering-fraud-proof}
    For an accepted authored act $q$, an \emph{ordering fraud proof} is the
    ordinary full opening $\fraudproof{q}=\bigl(\actid{q},\actdeps{q},
    \actdepsalt{q}\bigr)$ of its dependency projection; the finalized act
    already supplies $\precommit{q}$, $\actdepscommit{q}$, the host
    verification seal, the approval witness, and the authoritative order.  Anyone
    verifies the opening,
    \[
        H\!\left(\textsf{PN-dependency-v1}\parallel\actid{q}
        \parallel \precommit{q}\parallel \actdepsalt{q}
        \parallel\operatorname{encode}(\actdeps{q})\right)=\actdepscommit{q},
    \]
    and then $\depok{k}{q}$
    (\zcref{def:graph:authoritative-act-order}).  The proof succeeds iff
    $\neg\depok{k}{q}$ --- some dependency is absent from the
    finalized history or shares the epoch at authoritative time not strictly
    below $q$.  A fraud proof reveals the complete dependency list; there is no
    selective disclosure or zero-knowledge mechanism.  The projection thus gives
    privacy while unopened and public accountability when opened, and a later
    opening does not restore the Layer-1 projection to full state.
\end{definition}

\begin{postulate}[Ordering Accountability]
    \label{post:graph:ordering-accountability}
    The authoritative order remains semantically authoritative after
    finalization (\zcref{def:graph:authoritative-act-order}): it determines the
    finalized edge records, times, standing, and title.  A successful ordering
    fraud proof (\zcref{def:graph:ordering-fraud-proof}) establishes only that
    the host finalized an Actor-approved act while violating the dependency list
    committed into it.  It may trigger fault attribution, operator slashing, or
    sanctions under the deployment mechanism, but it does not reorder the epoch,
    delete the act or its records, reverse action counts or debits, recompute
    historical standing, or reverse title.  The specification therefore
    distinguishes the \emph{authoritative} order (which fixes finalized state)
    from a \emph{compliant} order (which satisfies every committed dependency):
    an order can be authoritative yet later be proven non-compliant.  By
    finalizing $q$ the host attests it received and validated the full dependency
    opening and chose an order satisfying it; it cannot defend a fraud proof by
    claiming it never held the list.
\end{postulate}

\begin{postulate}[Act Authentication Requirements]
    \label{post:graph:act-authentication-requirements}
    Before an authored act becomes eligible for the authoritative
    sequence, the deployment must provide all of:
    \begin{enumerate}[nosep,label=(\roman*)]
        \item \textbf{authorship:}
              publicly checkable evidence that the stated Actor
              authorized the proposal;
        \item \textbf{proposal integrity:}
              a host cannot substitute another structural body, removable
              payload projection, dependency projection, or requested
              publication state without detection;
        \item \textbf{realization transparency:}
              every host-added field of the finalizable act is visible to
              the Actor before final approval;
        \item \textbf{exact approval:}
              only the exact finalizable act approved by the Actor may
              enter the authoritative sequence;
        \item \textbf{hyper-act unity:}
              both projections of a hyper-edge resolve to the same
              approved parent act;
        \item \textbf{removable-projection binding:}
              removing an opening does not permit the immutable act to be
              rebound to another payload or dependency value;
        \item \textbf{ordering accountability:}
              where dependency compliance is claimed, public evidence can
              establish a violation without rewriting finalized history.
    \end{enumerate}
\end{postulate}

\begin{remark}[Authentication Realization Is Out of Scope]
    \label{rem:graph:authentication-realization-out-of-scope}
    This specification prescribes the properties of authenticated act
    formation, not a cryptographic realization.  Signature schemes,
    commitment schemes, hash functions, salts, serialization formats, key
    management, proof encodings, and algorithm migration are deployment
    concerns.  Any implementation satisfying
    \zcref{post:graph:act-authentication-requirements} is compliant.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Act Finalization Epoch]
    \label{def:graph:act-finalization-epoch}
    For any authored act $q$,
    $\operatorname{ep}(q) = \min\set{k : q \in \actsequence{k}}$ --- well-defined
    by monotonicity of the accepted act history and the epoch edge sets
    (\zcref{post:introduction:epoch-edge-set}). Two acts are \emph{co-epochal}
    iff their finalization epochs are equal. Title consumes acts at
    $\operatorname{ep}(\cdot)$ granularity only.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Settlement Recognition]
    \label{def:graph:settlement-recognition}
    \necessityref{subsec:necessity:epoch-quantized-consent}%
    A \emph{settlement candidate} on Item~$n_i$ in epoch edge set~$E_k$ is
    a triple of authored acts
    $\settlement = (q_{\mathrm{Bid}}, q_{\mathrm{Accept}}, q_{\mathrm{Ratify}})$
    whose Accept and Ratify both carry settlement act references
    (\zcref{def:graph:settlement-act-reference}) resolving to the Bid act
    identifier that opened the Offer.  The candidate is \emph{recognized}
    iff all six clauses hold:
    \begin{enumerate}[nosep, label=(\roman*)]
        \item \textbf{Completeness.} All three acts are present, their edge
              projections in~$E_k$.
        \item \textbf{Reference binding.} The Accept's and Ratify's settlement
              references both resolve to the Bid act identifier
              $\actid{q_{\mathrm{Bid}}}$.
          \item \textbf{Authorization.} The author of the Accept is the
              certified owner $\titlecert{k-1}(n_i)$ at the boundary
              preceding the Ratify's finalization epoch
              $k = \operatorname{ep}(\mathrm{Ratify})$ (the genesis owner
              if the thread is fresh).
          \item \textbf{Buyer consent.} No buyer Withdraw on this Offer has
              $\operatorname{ep}(\mathrm{Withdraw}) \le
               \operatorname{ep}(\mathrm{Ratify})$.
          \item \textbf{Seller consent.} No seller Rescind on this Offer has
              $\operatorname{ep}(\mathrm{Rescind}) \le
               \operatorname{ep}(\mathrm{Ratify})$.
          \item \textbf{Well-formedness.}
              $\mathrm{Bid} \prec \mathrm{Accept} \prec \mathrm{Ratify}$ ---
              retained as a well-formedness check on the handshake chain
              (each party observes the prior record); it carries no
              tie-breaking force.
    \end{enumerate}
        Clauses~(iv) and~(v) are the \emph{epoch-quantized consent rule}: a
        cancellation co-epochal with, or earlier than, the commit defeats it;
        a cancellation in a strictly later epoch is inert (the sale is final
        at the certificate). Consent must be live \emph{through the boundary},
        because nothing binds before it
        (\zcref{subsec:necessity:epoch-quantized-consent}). A recognized
        candidate whose Ratify finalizes at boundary~$k$ with no defeating
        cancel is \emph{unchallenged at~$k$}. Parallel settlement records are
        consumed exclusively through this predicate
        (\zcref{rem:graph:authored-act-bundle-consumers}).
\end{definition}

    \begin{remark}[Title Reads the Chain and the Epoch, Not Host Discretion]
        \label{rem:graph:title-order-irrelevance}
        Title separates cleanly from the host's residual ordering discretion.
        Handshake \emph{well-formedness} is fixed by the public,
        non-tombstonable settlement references (Accept names the Bid, Ratify
        names the same Bid and the exact Accept,
        \zcref{def:graph:public-protocol-reference,def:graph:settlement-act-reference}):
        because those references are declared dependencies, any authoritative
        order necessarily places $\mathrm{Bid}\prec\mathrm{Accept}\prec
        \mathrm{Ratify}$, so $\acttime{\mathrm{Bid}}<\acttime{\mathrm{Accept}}<
        \acttime{\mathrm{Ratify}}$ is forced, not host-chosen.  \emph{Conflict
        resolution} reads only set membership, $\operatorname{ep}(\cdot)$
        indices, and that chain --- never the residual sub-epoch positions of
        unconstrained acts or the tombstonable dependency projection. Closure
        selection is equally invisible: the rule
        (\zcref{post:epoch:final-act-sequence-closure}) decides membership only --- never
        recognition, tie-breaking, or scoring. There is consequently nothing for
        a host to decide by its residual sequencing and nothing for an author to
        gain by time-stuffing --- the two horns of the retired ordering dilemma.
        The host's sole title-relevant power is epoch membership itself,
        governed by \zcref{post:graph:boundary-accountability}; the certificate
        makes the written partition replayable, so validity is auditable where
        sequencing never was.
    \end{remark}

    \begin{postulate}[Boundary Accountability]
        \label{post:graph:boundary-accountability}
        The boundary mechanism satisfies three obligations. First, the
        certificate publishes the constraints and the dependent-set partition of
        $\actsequence{k}$, so validity of every written set is replayable against
        \zcref{post:epoch:final-act-sequence-closure}. Second, each
        certificate carries an attested boundary timestamp and its closure cause
        (target or duration), so the published epoch durations
        (\zcref{post:network:host-contract}) are auditable against the record.
        Third, no record class carries a write right. Selection among valid
        writes remains boundary discretion; the evidence-bearing object is the
        certificate against the published policy, not an audit of the unwritten.
    \end{postulate}


\begin{remark}[Clause Structure]
    \label{rem:graph:settlement-clause-structure}
    Clauses~(i),(ii) are set-membership and pointer-resolution predicates;
    (iii) reads the prior certificate; (iv),(v) compare finalization-epoch
    indices; (vi) is a well-formedness chain check. No clause reads
    $\logpos{e}$, sub-epoch order, or Lamport comparability.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Ownership Thread]
    \label{def:graph:ownership-thread}
    The \emph{ownership thread} of Item~$n_i$ is the boundary-indexed
    chain rooted at the genesis record (\zcref{def:graph:item-genesis-act})
    and extended at each epoch boundary by the title fold of
    \zcref{thm:graph:epoch-title-fold}. Its terminal actor is the
    certified owner. An Owner record not reachable from the genesis
    through boundary transfers is \emph{orphaned}: it persists in the
    append-only record set but carries no title force.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Settlement Consumption]
    \label{def:graph:settlement-consumption}
    Let $C_k(n_i)$ be the set of recognized, unchallenged candidates on
    Item~$n_i$ whose Ratify finalizes at boundary~$k$. Every member of
    $C_k(n_i)$ is \emph{consumed at~$k$}: whatever the fold's outcome,
    consumed records are permanently ineligible to found recognition at
    any later boundary. Retrying a failed purchase requires fresh
    records, each a priced act.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Title Certificate]
    \label{def:graph:title-certificate}
    The title certificate at epoch~$k$ is the map
    $\titlecert{k}\!: \text{Items} \to V_u \cup \set{\void}$ sending each
    Item to the terminal actor of its ownership thread, or to~$\void$ if
    no genesis Owner edge resolves it.  Layer~1 publishes $\titlecert{k}$
    alongside the epoch certificate
    (\zcref{post:epoch:final-edge-set}).
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Epoch Title Fold]
    \label{thm:graph:epoch-title-fold}
    \necessityref{subsec:necessity:mutual-consumption}%
    At each boundary~$k$, for each Item~$n_i$: if $|C_k(n_i)| = 1$,
    title transfers to that candidate's buyer; if $|C_k(n_i)| \ge 2$
    (conflicting same-epoch commits from one owner), \textbf{all members
    are consumed without transfer} and the incumbent retains title ---
    mutual invalidation, not permanence: the Item remains fully
    transferable at every later boundary. If $C_k(n_i) = \void$, title
    is unchanged.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
    $C_k(n_i)$ is a function of $(E_{k-1}, E_k, \titlecert{k-1})$ alone:
    recognition clauses (i)--(v) read set membership and
    $\operatorname{ep}(\cdot)$ indices, and clause~(iii) reads the prior
    certificate. Induction over boundaries grounds at the genesis
    record. Conflicts are exactly co-epochal authorized commits; the
    consumption rule resolves them without any intra-epoch order, and
    consumed candidates cannot recur by
    \zcref{def:graph:settlement-consumption}. A candidate whose Ratify
    lands one epoch after a competitor's transfer fails clause~(iii)
    (the owner changed) and is not recognized --- \emph{first epoch
    wins; ties consume}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The Regret Window]
    \label{rem:graph:regret-window}
    Under epoch quantization the Ratify is no longer the point of no
    return; the \emph{certificate} is. Either party retains the opportunity
    to cancel co-epochally with the commit, subject to inclusion
    (\zcref{rem:graph:cancellation-best-effort}) --- including a seller who has
    already seen the Ratify. This is deliberate and symmetric: nothing binds
    before the boundary, so consent is live exactly as long as commitment is
    pending, and reneging is a public, priced, reputation-bearing act
    (\zcref{rem:graph:settlement-reputation}). Settlement finality latency is
    bounded by the epoch closure rule (timeout rail; calibration commit).
    Layer-2 escrows key on the certificate, never the Ratify record
    (\zcref{rem:graph:settlement-cross-layer}).
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Cancellation Is Best-Effort]
    \label{rem:graph:cancellation-best-effort}
    Cancellation is expressible whenever its author clears the universal gates,
    and effective only if included at or before the commit's finalization epoch.
    The network guarantees the boundary, never delivery, in the register of
    \zcref{ins:introduction:the-floor-we-name}. Sharp form: ties favor the
    cancel (\zcref{def:graph:settlement-recognition}, clauses~(iv)--(v)), so any
    cancel submitted in an epoch strictly before the commit's finalization epoch
    is safe regardless of latency; the frontier buffer slides near-cutoff races
    into a tie, which the cancel wins. The exposure is exactly the last-epoch
    tail: commit landed, cancel after cutoff. Early regret is reliable regret.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Order-Freeness of Title]
    \label{thm:graph:settlement-order-freeness}
    Fix~$E_k$.  Then settlement recognition
    (\zcref{def:graph:settlement-recognition}), the ownership thread
    (\zcref{def:graph:ownership-thread}), and the title certificate
    (\zcref{def:graph:title-certificate}) are functions of the epoch partition
    $\set{E_j}_{j\le k}$ and the reference-forced well-formedness chain
    (clause~(vi), \zcref{rem:graph:title-order-irrelevance}) alone --- a strictly
    stronger invariance than ordered-replay determinism: the host's residual
    sub-epoch ordering of unconstrained acts enters nowhere. The settlement
    protocol introduces \textbf{no new order-sensitive quantity};
    $\set{\burnval{i}}$ remains the sole boundary-state residual
    (\attestationcref{prop:invariants:burn-order-residual}).
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
    Clauses~(i)--(v) are set/index predicates; clause~(iii) recurses
    through prior certificates to the genesis record. The fold is
    \zcref{thm:graph:epoch-title-fold}. No step references $\logpos{e}$,
    $\idorder$, or sub-epoch order.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[No Death-by-Inaction]
    \label{thm:graph:no-death-by-inaction}
    \necessityref{subsec:necessity:explicit-cancels}%
    Every transition out of a non-terminal settlement state is caused by an
    authored edge; the lifecycle map $E_k \mapsto \mathrm{state}(\settlement)$
    depends on no count, window, or throughput measure.  No settlement
    state changes through the absence of an edge, and the protocol carries
    no $T_{\mathrm{bid}}$ analogue.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
    The transitions are: Open$\to$Accepted (Accept, seller); Open$\to$Dead
    (Withdraw, buyer); Accepted$\to$Committed (Ratify, buyer);
    Accepted$\to$Dead (Withdraw, buyer); Accepted$\to$Dead (Rescind,
    seller).  Each is labeled by an authored edge; Dead and Committed are
    absorbing; persistence in Open or Accepted is the absence of any such
    edge and yields no transition.  ``Stays forever'' is harmless: no
    pre-commit state locks value (escrow is Layer~2, funded at Ratify) and
    no pre-commit state is binding.  Cleanup is an authored choice ---
    Withdraw or Rescind --- never a silent push onto the counterparty.
    The boundary fold introduces no timeout: consumption at a boundary is
    caused by the conflicting authored records themselves, evaluated at
    the next global progress point --- a legitimate uniform measure
    (\zcref{rem:graph:causal-locality-principle}), never a per-object clock.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Causal-Locality Principle]
    \label{rem:graph:causal-locality-principle}
    No \emph{per-object} state transition may be triggered by that
    object's own inaction.  Global progress measures (frontier
    stability~$\snapbuf$, the Layer~0 maturity lead $\matlead$, epoch
    length~$\epochlen$) are legitimate --- they gate all objects uniformly
    by system-wide advancement.  A per-object timeout (``Bid expires after
    $T_{\mathrm{bid}}$ epochs'') would make a Bid's death depend on
    unrelated global throughput, a negative-evidence transition the causal
    structure cannot represent.  Explicit cancels keep every death incident
    to the dying object's Offer.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Settlement Reputation: the Stance Conjunction]
    \label{rem:graph:settlement-reputation}
    Three authored edges carry three signed stances --- the directional
    roles $\operatorname{sgn}(g_{\mathrm{Bid}})$ (buyer's stance: generous
    vs.\ predatory), $\operatorname{sgn}(c_{\mathrm{Acc}})$ (seller's
    experience: comfortable vs.\ coerced), and
    $\operatorname{sgn}(c_{\mathrm{Rat}})$ (buyer's confirmation:
    satisfied vs.\ reluctant). \textbf{Title transfer is
    sentiment-independent}: a structurally valid, title-transferring settlement
    transfers title regardless of sign, so ``I was uncomfortable'' is not
    a repudiation exploit. \textbf{Commercial reputation is gated by the
    stance conjunction}: positive reputation iff all three stance
    marginals are positive. The conjunction reads the \emph{stance}
    ($p_d$ role, published in the always-active marginal row
    $\fpm{p_d}$, verifiable at $O(1)$), \emph{not} the bilinear parity
    $\detsign{e}$: by the Quadrant Law
    (\zcref{lem:graph:quadrant-law}) the parity is
    $\operatorname{sgn}(p_dp_i)$, so a coerced \emph{and} unfair Accept
    ($c < 0$, $e < 0$) carries $\detsign{} = +1$ --- correct for
    routing coherence, and exactly wrong as a reputation verdict.
    Routing reads coherence; reputation reads stance --- the dual-view
    discrimination/equity split, applied to sign. For the Bid the two
    readings coincide ($u \geq 0$ forces
    $\detsign{e_{\mathrm{Bid}}} = \operatorname{sgn}(g)$,
    \zcref{cor:nodes:bid-leg-parity}). Nor is the conjunction the parity
    product $\prod\detsign{e}$, which would reward
    predatory-meets-coerced. The same stance law gates standing: an
    Accept or Ratify enters the standing projection only when its own
    record satisfies the Vouch Predicate (\zcref{def:epoch:effective-act-contribution}).
    Thus the coerced-and-unfair record $(c<0,e<0)$ remains coherent for routing
    parity but contributes neither positive commercial reputation nor
    standing flow.  The raw signed double-cover service itself remains
    recognition-blind and unchanged; the vouch filter is applied in the
    standing projection.  The residual injection question is therefore narrowed to
    \emph{stance-positive} fabricated ties, and is recorded at
    \zcref{frontier:settlement-tie-fabrication}.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Reviews Are Commentary, Never State]
    \label{rem:graph:reviews-commentary}
    Every passive node type implements Reviewable
    (\zcref{tbl:nodes:affordance-traits}): anything that exists in the
    graph admits attributed public commentary --- the accountability-cost
    posture (\zcref{post:comparator:accountability-cost}) applied
    universally. A Review is commentary on its target and nothing else:
    it transitions no settlement state, moves no title, binds no tag,
    creates no membership, and enters no admission quantity
    (\zcref{def:network:admission-closure}); the only edges that
    transition settlement state remain Bid, Accept, Ratify, Withdraw,
    and Rescind (\zcref{def:graph:settlement-recognition}).

    Universal Reviewable also \emph{allocates to no person}, and that is
    semantic rather than topological.  A Review is still weighed, and
    weighed home (\zcref{def:epoch:standing-recipient-resolution}); what it
    is not is a family that can carry allocation outward.  No raw Review leg or
    Review-created Comment can lend upstream standing to a third
    party's later Reference: a later Reference is evaluated as its own
    complete act and through its own author
    (\zcref{def:graph:act-edge-projection,%
    rem:graph:grounded-target-does-not-imply-allocation}).
    Thus public commentary remains available to feed, CAN, and terminal
    guild policies without becoming a standing conduit.  For the
    Offer in particular, reviews are consumable by Layer~2 reputation,
    dispute, or display policies and are ignored by every recognition
    clause; a control edge followed by an Offer's Review/T leg forms a
    path whose weight product ($\lesssim 10^{-3}$) sits an order of
    magnitude below the weakest legitimate two-hop \tiermarginal{} chain
    already tolerated by \zcref{cor:scalability:spam-resistance}.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Settlement Cross-Layer Protocol]
    \label{rem:graph:settlement-cross-layer}
    Layer~1 holds no value, locks nothing, adjudicates nothing; it records
    Offers and ownership changes.  A Layer~2 escrow observes the public
    log: buyer Bids (Offer created); buyer funds escrow keyed to the Offer
    identity (reversible); seller verifies funding; seller Accepts; buyer
    Ratifies; \textbf{the boundary finalizes}; escrow observes the first
    epoch certificate in which the settlement is recognized, unchallenged,
    and title-transferring (\zcref{thm:graph:epoch-title-fold}) and releases.
    The certificate is the point of no return: an immutable event under
    \zcref{post:introduction:public-accessibility,post:introduction:record-integrity},
    it is the deterministic event an honest escrow keys against.  This is
    not cross-layer atomicity --- a value-free registry cannot guarantee
    the seller is paid, and a suppressed cancel leaves no Layer-1 evidence
    capable of restoring title --- but a \textbf{deterministic commit anchor},
    mirroring Layer~0's split between protocol costliness
    (\attestationcref{thm:interface:instantaneous-costliness}) and market
    discipline (\attestationcref{sec:discipline}).
\end{remark}

\begin{algorithm}
        \caption{Title-Certificate Computation (boundary fold). A function of
        the epoch partition; order-free by
        \zcref{thm:graph:settlement-order-freeness}. Incremental per boundary
        in deployment; stated as a full replay for verification.}
    \label{alg:graph:title-certificate-computation}
    \begin{algorithmic}[1]
         \State \textbf{Input:} epoch partition $\set{E_j}_{j \le k}$
         \State $\titlecert{0}(\cdot) \gets$ genesis owners
             \Comment{\zcref{def:graph:item-genesis-act}; $\void$ if none}
         \For{$j = 1$ \textbf{to} $k$}
             \ForAll{Items $n_i$ with $C_j(n_i) \neq \void$}
              \If{$|C_j(n_i)| = 1$}
                  \State $\titlecert{j}(n_i) \gets$ buyer of the sole
                      candidate
              \Else
                  \State consume all of $C_j(n_i)$; title unchanged
                      \Comment{\zcref{thm:graph:epoch-title-fold}}
              \EndIf
            \EndFor
        \EndFor
        \State \Return $\titlecert{k}$
    \end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\section{Nodes and Edges}
\label{sec:nodes}

% ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
\subsection{Universal Principles}
\label{subsec:nodes:universal-principles}
% ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

\marginpar{\footnotesize \zcref{tbl:nodes:archetype-fingerprints}
(Archetype Fingerprints) summarises all edge types.}

All edges and hyper-edges adhere to seven structural invariants:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
    \item Every edge carries a local time integer $\acttime{\actof{e}}$ and
          maturity scalar $\tau_e$
          (\zcref{ax:graph:act-causality}).
    \item Every edge's stored sentiment is a $3 \times 3$ extended
          slice $\symbf{\Psi}_e$ constructed via the canonical
          pipeline (\zcref{post:nodes:canonical-tensor-pipeline}).
    \item Every edge exposes three computational interfaces
          (\zcref{def:graph:dual-view-architecture}): scalar,
          \PathView{}, \AttrView{}.
    \item Every hyper-edge decomposes into an A-leg and a T-leg for raw
          graph and CAN consumers
          (\zcref{thm:graph:hyper-edge-reduction}).  A standing-designated
          hyper-edge is different: standing consumes the matched pair once
          as one complete act, never as independently reachable legs
          (\zcref{cor:graph:standing-act-atomicity}).
    \item Boundary damping $\boltzfactor{\tentropy{}}$ is applied at
          observation, not to stored tensors
          (\zcref{ax:epoch:thermodynamic-boundary}).
        \item Every authored act carries a payload commitment
            (\zcref{def:graph:act-payload-projection}); payload bytes and state are
            terminal and enter the canonical pipeline nowhere
            (\zcref{prop:graph:removable-projection-invariance}).  Nodes carry
            nothing: every node-level quantity is a declared fold over
            incident records
            (\zcref{ax:graph:authored-act-ontology,def:graph:canonical-folds}).
    \item Standing authority is assigned by the closed census of
          \zcref{def:epoch:standing-recipient-resolution}.  Positive determinant
          parity, a grounded target, a strong raw edge weight, or a
          passive artifact's incoming weight is never sufficient by itself
          to create a person-vouch.
\end{enumerate}

All nodes are partitioned into $V_u$ (active) and $V_c$ (passive).
In the \ActionGraph{}, every record is authored by an active node;
passive nodes never autonomously originate or
redirect an edge (\zcref{ax:graph:passivity}). A passive node may source
author-fixed outgoing edges --- the terminal leg of each hyper-edge in
which it is the middle node, and (for Profile nodes only) the
derived Reputation component
(\zcref{lem:graph:passive-out-degree}). Each node participates in the
dual-view architecture through the edges it anchors:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
    \item \textbf{\PathView{}:} incident edges' path-view
          determinants govern path routing. \tierfull{} edges make the
          node a strong routing element; \tiermarginal{} edges contribute
          weakly.
    \item \textbf{\AttrView{}:} incident edges' $3 \times 3$
          Frobenius norms provide CAN base values, nearly equalized
            across edge types ($\sim\!21\%$ full-range variation).
    \item \textbf{Scalar:} a passive node's aggregate
          $\norm{\symbf{\symcal{T}}_c}_F$ enters the relevance
          score (\zcref{def:sorting:relevance-score}).
\end{itemize}

\begin{postulate}[Canonical Tensor Pipeline]
    \label{post:nodes:canonical-tensor-pipeline}
    \deploymentref{subsec:deployment:sufficiency}%
    For every edge $e$ (binary or hyper-edge leg):
    \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
        \item \textbf{Role assignment.} Domain-specific parameters
              are assigned to directional ($p_d$) and intensity
              ($p_i$) roles. Single-parameter edges set the missing
              role to~$1$.
        \item \textbf{Extended slice.} $\symbf{\Psi}_e$ is computed
              via the master formula
              (\zcref{def:graph:sentiment-slice}) with the domain's
              bilinear mask.
        \item \textbf{Path-view extraction.} $\pathview{e}$ is
              extracted with $\bleedparam$-softening
              (\zcref{def:graph:path-view-extraction}).
        \item \textbf{Temporal augmentation.}
              $\symbf{\symcal{T}}_e
              = \symbf{\Psi}_e \boxtimes (1, \tau_e)^T$.
        \item \textbf{Interface extraction.}
              Scalar: $\norm{\symbf{\Psi}_e}_F \cdot
              \sqrt{1+\tau_e^2}$.
              \PathView{}: $\pathview{e}$.
              \AttrView{}: $\norm{\symbf{\Psi}_e}_F$.
    \end{enumerate}
\end{postulate}

\begin{remark}[Single-Parameter Row Collapse]
    \label{rem:nodes:row-collapse}
    Step~1's rule --- single-parameter edges set the missing role
    to~$1$ --- makes rows $g{=}1,2$ of the stored slice coincide for Owner
    and Send/A (the $\svdthree{} = 0$ corner of
    \zcref{prop:graph:rank-two-constraint}). The duplicated row modestly
    inflates the \AttrView{} norm --- Owner's $\numval{result.e8.frobenius.num}$ is the census
    maximum partly for this reason --- but within the $\sim\!16\%$
    equity band the dual-view split already tolerates, and the collapse
    \emph{improves} the rank-2 approximation the path view rests on.
    Decisively, parameter count is type-fixed, never user-electable: no
    actor can drop a parameter to harvest the duplication, so the
    inflation is a census property, not an incentive surface.
\end{remark}

% ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
\subsection{Standing Roles Under Universal Weighing}
\label{subsec:nodes:standing-recipient-resolution}
% ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Edition~4 carried a normative census here: a table assigning each raw edge
family and complete act one of three standing roles, so that a reader could
look up whether a given record carried standing at all.

Universal act weighing dissolves the question
(\zcref{post:epoch:universal-act-weighing}).  Every accepted Actor-authored
act is weighed exactly once; nothing is exempt and nothing is privileged.  What
remains is not \emph{whether} an act counts but \emph{towards whom}, and that
is recipient resolution, which belongs with the standing model rather than with
the record taxonomy (\zcref{def:epoch:standing-recipient-resolution,%
tbl:epoch:standing-recipient-resolution}).

The taxonomy survives where it always belonged, as a statement about records:
raw derived edges remain raw, a complete hyper-edge is consumed as one act
(\zcref{cor:graph:standing-act-atomicity}), and passive artifacts author
nothing.  None of that is a standing role; it is what the projection means.

\paragraph{Self-resolution is not inertness.}
The blocks below describe what each family does, and a reader pricing their
own activity from them should carry one fact into every entry.  An act that
allocates to no person is \textbf{not} standing-inert: it is weighed, at its
own coefficient, and it lands on its author's self-retention.  Because the
row is conserved, that weight is subtracted from everything the author sends
outward (\zcref{rem:epoch:artifact-activity-crowds-out-export}).  Tagging,
reviewing, bidding, sending, registering and publishing are therefore not
free with respect to standing --- they are the ordinary price of acting, paid
out of the same single unit that endorsements are paid from.

This is the reading Edition~4 got the other way round, and getting it
backwards is expensive: an Actor who believes artifact activity is inert will
under-price their whole act mix.  Nothing below says ``no standing'' about an
accepted act, and where a family genuinely carries none it is because the
record is not an authored act at all.

\begin{remark}[Coherence Does Not Assign the Standing Role]
    \label{rem:nodes:coherence-does-not-allocate}
    The determinant sign remains a raw coherence bit
    (\zcref{rem:graph:sign-semantics}).  It neither adds a family to
    \zcref{tbl:epoch:standing-recipient-resolution} nor redirects a
    self-resolving act outward.  In particular:
    \begin{itemize}[nosep]
        \item a positive-parity Tag, Review, Bid, Send, or control
              record still resolves home, and is weighed there;
        \item a coherent-hostile $(-,-)$ person-directed act still
              resolves home, at its own magnitude
              (\zcref{rem:epoch:hostility-is-priced});
        \item an unmatched positive T-leg is not a complete act and
              contributes nothing anywhere;
        \item a complete positive person-vouch still requires the
              family-specific epoch fold before projection.
    \end{itemize}
\end{remark}

% ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
\subsection{Affordance Traits}
\label{subsec:nodes:affordance-traits}
% ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Node capabilities are governed by abstract traits specifying which
hyper-edges a node type can anchor.

\begin{table}[h!]
    \caption{Node affordance traits.}
    \label{tbl:nodes:affordance-traits}
    \centering
    \begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}l X >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
        \toprule
        \textbf{Trait} & \textbf{Description}
            & \textbf{Implemented By} \\
        \midrule
        \textbf{Taggable}
            & Target of a Tag hyper-edge.
            & Profile, Content, Item, Type, Chat,
              Comment, Message. \\
        \addlinespace
        \textbf{Reviewable}
                        & Target of a Review hyper-edge; sources the author-fixed
                            Review/T leg to the created Comment.
                        & All passive types: Profile, Content, Item, Type,
                            Chat, Comment, Message, Offer (universal;
                            \zcref{rem:graph:reviews-commentary}). \\
        \addlinespace
        \textbf{Ownable}
            & Target of Owner and Bid edges.
            & Item. \\
        \addlinespace
        \textbf{Conversational}
                        & Target of Join Request and Leave edges; middle node of
                            Invitation, De-invite, and Send hyper-edges.
            & Chat. \\
        \bottomrule
    \end{tabularx}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Target validity.}
Opinion targets any passive node; Affinity targets Type; Tag targets
Taggable; Review targets Reviewable; Registration targets Profile;
Publish targets Content; Owner and Bid target Ownable; Join
Request, Invitation/A, Send/A, Leave, De-invite/A, and Participant/A target
Chat; Participant/T targets Chat; Withdraw and Rescind target Offer; Invitation/T targets the invitee's
Profile; De-invite/T targets the de-invitee's Profile.  The T-leg terminus of
a minting family is typed too: Review/T targets Comment, Send/T targets
Message, and Bid/T targets Offer.  A payload on any edge
does not make the edge or its target a Content node: content candidacy and
rendering are Layer~2 selections over payload-bearing incident edges.

\paragraph{Freshness of the terminal target.}
Target validity types the terminal target; it does not require that target to
be fresh.  For \textbf{Publish}, \textbf{Owner}, \textbf{Review/T} and
\textbf{Send/T} the terminus may equally be the act's own mint or a node that
already exists, and formation decides which by comparing two fields of the
one act (\zcref{def:graph:genesis-act-and-creator}).  This is what makes an
update expressible at all: records are immutable, so revising a node can only
mean authoring a further record about it.

\textbf{Bid/T} is the exception and is \emph{fresh-mint-only}.  An Offer's
provenance from a single Item is assumed by the settlement lifecycle, and a
